title: Building a close board fence with arris rails and posts
subtitle: Erect a privacy fence using concrete posts, triangular arris rails, and vertical featheredge boards
excerpt: How to build a traditional close-board fence with concrete posts, triangular arris rails, and featheredge boards. Covers setting post positions, concreting posts, fixing arris rails, and nailing the boards.
sourceNotes: Collins Complete DIY Manual (referenced, not reproduced). UK fencing trade practice.

glossaryTerms.definition: A triangular-section horizontal rail, typically 75 x 75 mm softwood with a triangular cross-section. The flat base of the triangle sits on the post mortise or mortise cup and the sloping top face throws water clear. Featheredge boards nail to the two sloping faces of the arris rail. Two arris rails span between each pair of posts: one near the top and one near the bottom.

A timber privacy fence in which vertical featheredge boards overlap each other by 10 to 15 mm, so no light passes through the fence. Boards are fixed to horizontal arris rails spanning between posts. Close-board fencing gives more rigidity and privacy than panel fencing and is more resistant to wind damage.

content.text: uses vertical featheredge boards nailed to horizontal
spanning between posts. It is stronger than panel fencing and each component can be replaced individually. A standard bay is 1.8 m wide between post centres and 1.8 m tall.
Set out and install the posts

Mark post positions with a garden cane at 1.8 m centres along the fence line. For a 1.8 m-tall fence, concrete posts are typically 2.4 m long: 600 mm goes in the ground, 1.8 m above. Dig post holes 600 mm deep with a post-hole borer or a spade. Concrete posts have pre-mortised holes for the arris rail ends. Mix post concrete to a stiff consistency and pour around the post, tamping it in. Check plumb on two adjacent faces with the spirit level. Prop the post with temporary battens until the concrete sets (at least 24 hours before loading with arris rails).

Arris rails span between posts and locate in the mortise slots. On concrete posts, slot the arris rail ends into the pre-cast mortise cups. For a 1.8 m fence, fit a top rail about 200 mm from the top of the posts and a bottom rail about 200 mm from the ground. Cut arris rails to length with the crosscut saw: a 1.8 m bay requires rails about 1.85 m long to allow for the mortise seating. Nail the arris rail into timber posts with 100 mm galvanised wire nails through the mortise; concrete posts have the arris rail fixed by the cup only.

Start from one post and nail the first featheredge board with its thick edge outward (facing outward from the garden). Use a 6 to 10 mm overlap guide (a batten or offcut) to set the consistent overlap on each successive board. Nail each board at the top and bottom arris rail with a single 65 mm stainless nail per rail, keeping the nail in the thick part of the board, not through the overlapping thin top edge of the board below. Check the boards plumb every three or four boards; featheredge boards will creep out of plumb if not checked regularly.

Fix a 100 x 25 mm capping rail along the tops of the boards by nailing down through the capping into each board. The capping protects the cut tops of the featheredge boards from rain and prevents lifting. Apply a coat of fence preservative or oil to the finished fence within the first month.

attrs.symptom: Posts lean after the first winter
attrs.cause: Post not concreted deep enough, or the concrete mix was too weak.
attrs.fix: 600 mm depth is the minimum for a 1.8 m fence post. In soft or clay soil, increase to 750 mm. Concrete to the surface and finish with a slight slope away from the post to shed water.

attrs.symptom: Boards warping and lifting off the arris rails
attrs.cause: Green timber used for the boards and not treated before installation.
attrs.fix: Replace warped boards with pre-treated or dried boards. Treat both faces, all four edges, and cut ends of all replacement boards before installation.
